BAASS has Contracted to Purchase
Information on UAPs from MUFON

      In order for BAASS to best serve the government it needs to become the
central information source on UAPs in the United States and around the world. It
is essential to receive information on current UAPs that are occurring in real time
in the United States until BAASS has sufficient staff (possibly 250 people ) and
other internal capabilities. One way for BAASS to achieve this goal is to contract
with an organization that has hundreds of investigators already in place around
the United States. The Mutual UFO Network (MUFON) is such an organization.
MUFON has been in existence for four decades and currently has approximately
1000 volunteers who can investigate reports of UAP sightings in all 50 states.

      In February 2009, BAASS executed a Purchase order with MUFON that
entitles BAASS to: (a) receive notification of significant reports on UAP sightings
from anywhere in the United States within hours, (b) receive timely reports from
MUFON investigators regarding investigations of these incidents (c) receive
physical evidence (including photographs, digital recordings, samples of soil,
insects, plants, and animals) for scientific analysis. BAASS has multiple
laboratories that are ready to conduct forensic, photographic, metallurgic,
chemical, isotope, biological, chemical analysis of any specimens that BAASS
receives from MUFON.

      BAASS has already hired a small team of ten high quality top investigators
with extensive intelligence and law enforcement investigative experience. These
investigators are currently located in Las Vegas and are trained to deploy as
"special forces" rapid reaction investigative teams that are deployable anywhere
in the United States if BAASS determines that high value UAP cases warrant
additional investigations. However this investigative group is still far too small to
even cover the geographic area needed in the United States, much less outside
this country.

      During the late evening hours of 30 Oct 75, several ground personnel reported seeing an airborne unidentified (reported as a helicopter) in the area of the perimeter of the base.

      Initially the sighting was near the base entry point in the Capeheart housing area. The personnel making the initial sightings were Security Police personnel. Based on the reported time of the incident (2200) these personnel would have been in the final hour of their shift. Security Police shifts normally ran during the following periods: 0700-1500; 1500-2300; 2300-0700. Shift change times, based on the above shifts, would have been 0630; 1430; and 2130. At these times the on duty shift would be preparing their posts for the oncoming personnel. The oncoming personnel would be drawing their weapons, preparing their vehicles and conducting inspections.

      Based on the reporting, the unidentified began its flight on the south-east side of the base and followed the perimeter, traveling to the north passing the main gate, where it was again sighted by the on duty gate guard. How this report is organized

This report consists of the present overview proposal and three appendices (two of which summarize previously-published work). Together, these four documents describe a consistent methodology for the capture, processing and retrieval of parameters characterizing unusual aerial phenomena and related anomalies. The appendices address three specific implementation areas, describing the technical choices we have made in each area and the reasons for these choices:

  - A. Classification methodology and reliability measures for reported sightings
  - B. Modeling of information categories, including high-strangeness data elements
  - C. Data Structures and Software Platforms in support of Aerial Phenomena Research

Given the tools described hereafter, some of which have already been implemented and tested in prototype form in the course of prior research, we examine several scenarios for the long-term acquisition, exploitation and maintenance of a comprehensive data warehousing system that could serve the needs of a geographically diverse research community with a wide variety of information needs.

In recent years, easy access to personal computers and the Internet has made it much easier for interested groups to start their own files. There are at least 30 active catalogues at various points of development, with obvious overlap and widely-varying standards. Special catalogues exist for material trace analysis, abduction claims, ancient sightings, and also for particular countries or regions. Several groups are active through closed Internet conferences and have begun to develop and exchange information through wikis in various languages. Furthermore, the range of available data sources has been expanded as countries like the U.K. and Spain followed the example of the U.S. Project Blue Book in releasing their declassified files, although not in an organized, structured computer-readable format.

  Lack of data validation and lack of standards has impeded progress among the researchers responsible for these databases. It is natural for people who have recently become aware of the field to launch into their own implementation of a file of selected cases in the hope of rapidly "solving" some of the problems raised by this puzzling phenomenon. Unfortunately, they rarely have the financial wherewithal or professional staff necessary to conduct field investigations or even elementary checks on the validity of the information they collect.

  As time goes on, unfortunately, this reinventing of the wheel fails to generate new results. Every group has implemented its own way of indexing, which makes it impractical, if not impossible, to exchange data. Furthermore, these groups have often used software techniques that were overly complex and hindered research and ease of access instead of promoting it: These catalogues rely on ambitious coding systems that demand large editing and updating efforts. As the implementers get older and are constrained by family or professional requirements they tend to move on and lose interest, and the files get abandoned for lack of trained staff to maintain the overall structure.


1. Implementation requirements


The new system to be developed needs (1) to support a family of catalogues of observations of unusual aerial phenomena whose nature or behavior suggest the presence of an unrecognized threat, (2) to be up and running within a short time, (3) to extend the search for such data to as many relevant regions of the world as possible to find out what knowledgeable researchers or authorities in those regions possess about such phenomena and (4) to allow sophisticated analyses and datamining to improve our own understanding of the extent, structure, and frequency of such events, as well as their potential correlation to known physical, environmental, biological or socio-political factors.

  The project should avoid the major pitfalls identified above. It should not require any special hardware or network scheme. It has to serve a closed community of physicists and analysts

AAP
Person 5          CAPELLA Data Warehouse          page 4

with the need to test certain theories (and counter-theories) about the nature of the phenomena involved. Therefore the work cannot be limited to data acquisition, indexing and storage but extends to the essential tasks of dynamic data validation and of providing the ability for users in the project environment to apply their own interactive screens against the data.
  The project should also be of service in contacting experts in other countries to validate certain findings from our teams and "drill down" deeper into certain hypotheses, archives or interesting sites around the world. Therefore it should be accessible anywhere through the Internet (under password protection when applicable).

  The software should make it easy to convert existing data into a single standard structure, to search for specific natural language expressions or keywords, to sort according to specific criteria and to support statistical tables and graphs.

  The system also must empower a community of researchers to propose and test their own hypotheses. Such testing is not possible today: Although many interesting theories have been advanced, they are limited by the poor selection of physical and social data available to us. The phenomenon is so diverse that any theory of it can be proven, provided one is free to select the "right" observations -- and ignore the rest! This is not good science, but in the absence of reliable data bases this selection bias is unavoidable. The large, scientifically-based effort that is contemplated here cannot afford to repeat the mistakes that, unfortunately, characterize the field.

  In summary, in order to accomplish all this, the system has to be portable, frugal, easily implemented on various computer platforms, without the need for a dedicated system team for maintenance or special programming.

A System of Classification and Reliability Indicators
for the Analysis of the Behavior

AAP Person 5

When faced with hundreds or even thousands of reports of unusual aerial phenomena, no serious researcher can undertake any study or hazard any hypothesis before analyzing the patterns buried in the reports. These patterns only reveal themselves when the witnesses' accounts are classified into major categories whose prevalence and recurrence can then be computed. This is a time-consuming task that demands a great deal of rigor, which explains why so few research organizations have done it consistently. In our own work, we have used such classification systems for many years, in the context of very different data sets. We have learned from early mistakes, and this effort has led us to propose the current scheme based on the reported behavior of the phenomenon under observation. The purpose of this paper is to clarify the system and its practical use.

And it must not presuppose any particular theory.

A Classification System based on the Behavior of the Phenomenon

The major flaw in previous classification systems is that they take as their basis the position of
the observer, which is arbitrary and changing, rather than the reported behavior of the
phenomenon from which one could draw important conclusions in terms of patterns. In other
words, it may be interesting to know that a particular witness described a disk while another saw
a triangle or a square, but this is a purely subjective item that is a function of the percipient, not a
behavioral attribute of the phenomenon: one person's "disk" is another person's "ball of light." It
is more relevant to know such stable facts as whether or not the object presented a discontinuity
in flight or came close to the ground, items for which there is more consistent agreement.
  Another flaw in existing systems is that they are too complicated and require constant reference
to codebooks with overly-detailed definitions that are time consuming and error-prone. In order
to encompass the full range of phenomena one finds in the reports from witnesses, it is important
to acknowledge that what most people call "UFOs" are related in significant ways to other
anomalies. It is the rule, rather than the exception, to find the observation of a flying object
preceded or followed by other unusual phenomena. For that reason, I find it useful to begin with a
classification of Anomalies that parallels 1843(a)  close encounter designations:
                                             (2)

AN1 events are anomalies like amorphous lights or unexplained explosions in the sky, that do
      not have lasting physical effects.
AN2 reports involve lasting physical effects, such as poltergeist phenomena, anomalous
      photographs, flattened grass or "apports."
AN3 cases are anomalies with associated entities. This could involve reports of ghosts and
      instances of crytozoology, or even "spirits."
AN4 designates those anomalous reports in which witnesses describe personal interaction with
      entities in the reality of the entities themselves. This includes near-death experiences,
      claims of religious visions and some cases of out-of-body experiences.

Finally, we place under AN5 the cases in which anomalous injuries or deaths are reported, such as unexplained wounds or spontaneous combustion. Claims of permanent healings would also fit within this category.

   We now come to the UFO reports themselves, which we will divide, following 1843(a)(2) into close encounters and distant sightings.

  We see no reason to change anything to the classification of close encounters that is in current use, from CE1 to CE4, although 1843(a)(2) was not responsible for creating the CE4 category and was not especially happy with this extension of his work. In recent years the need has arisen for a new category, CE5, which encompasses cases of close encounters in which the witnesses have suffered permanent injury or other physiological or pathological effects.

  Naturally, in introducing these classes of items, we make no assumption regarding the reality of the phenomenon as described by the witnesses, and we do not presuppose any physical explanation.

one another.  In the association between the sign "the coin" and its signified object, this

signified is arbitrary, the sign is referred to as a symbol.  With symbols, there is no intrinsic
connection between the form of expression (the sign) and the content that is expressed (the
signified).

symbols.  One alternative is the icon, a sign that bears a physical resemblance to the signified.
With icons, the form of the message reflects its contents.  For example, the profile of the man on
a modern American quarter is an icon for a specific man who was the first President of the
United States.  We can also represent the same man with the symbol "George Washington".  In
the former case, the image of Washington is an icon because it physically resembles the
signified.  Icons can also be used when the signified is less concrete.  For example, the scales of
justice icon represents the concept of justice because there is similarity between the sign (scales
that balance two weights) and the signified (concept of justice, which involves a balance between
transgression and punishment).

  Even such a complex scheme, however, fails to explain all the reported effects and the subsequent behavior changes in close-range witnesses. We must assume something more, the triggering of deep-seated processes within their personality. The question then becomes: to what extent are these effects evidence of a purposeful action of the operators? To answer this question, and to test more fully the hypothesis that UAP phenomena are both physical and psychic in nature, we need much better investigations, a great upgrading of data quality, and a more informed analysis not only of the object being described, but of the impact of the observation on the witnesses and their social environment.

Appendix C

Data Structures and Software Platforms
in support of Aerial Phenomena Research:
Proposed Organization, with examples

AAP Person 5
Documatica Research, LLC


The implementation of data bases for the purpose of research poses unusual challenges for the
software analyst. While an industrial database might consist of millions of items in a rapidly-
changing transaction environment, the data elements are well-defined and their characteristics
are fixed. For example, a database of parts for a car company will consist of elements where
composition, size, weight, price and availability are known at any given time. Furthermore, a
team of specialists is in charge of maintaining the database and optimizing it for specific
corporate departments whose requirements have been taken into account at the time of design.

 The situation is very different in research: Not all the questions to be posed can be defined at
the beginning of design; new elements, or novel ways of characterizing them, may appear in
the course of the project; there may be different user communities to be served; and even the
nature of the phenomenon under study may be in question. The problem of unexplained aerial
phenomena is of particular complexity, because the database must accommodate not only
initial hypotheses or mind frames of the designers, but those of future groups of users with
unpredictable requirements. Some of the users may be strong believers in a particular
interpretation of the data, or they may look for certain patterns, while researchers with
opposing views (or skeptics) will need to access the same data to creatively challenge their
colleagues' conclusions. The design must serve all these needs.

 In prior work the author and his colleagues have defined a general classification system for
reports based on the observed behavior of the phenomenon. This three-digit system was
adopted years ago by several catalogues, notably by NIDS in the 1990s, by UFOCAT (a
catalogue of the CUFOS organization) and by 1843(a)(2)     in France in support of his

AAP
Person 5                    Appendix C                    page 1

catalogue of pilot sightings. We propose to use it as one of the elements in the present work
(see definitions in Appendix A).

  In the same work we also established an "SVP" code for reliability indicators, tracking (S)
the level of the source for the data, (V) the degree to which the site was visited or inspected
and (P) the probability for a conventional explanation of the reported facts. This system is
also described in detail in Appendix A.

  The combination of the classification system and the reliability indicators enables a given
user to define his or her own "screen" to place over the data to select a particular sample or
subset of interest, or to split a catalogue into parts to be compared statistically against one
another – an operation that is usually impossible in most extant catalogues because behavior
and reliability are not clearly indicated.

  More recently, AAP Person 58  and the author have proposed a six-layer system for the
analysis of the phenomenon. This system (given in Appendix B) separates the various
elements of the witnesses' narrative into sections that are relevant to specific scientific
disciplines, from physics to medicine and psychology. Accordingly, the data structure we
have defined is implemented in Excel in the form of ten pages or screens, which can be
consulted and searched together, locally or globally. Each page is self-contained and designed
to be printed out separately if needed.

Conclusion


The requirements of a searchable, portable, easily-accessible series of databases capturing all
six layers of information about unexplained aerial phenomena can be satisfied with a
comprehensive data structure using nothing more complex than Microsoft Excel. The
proposed 10-page structure, which can be started with a single page and expanded later as
information is reviewed or becomes available, has already been tested on several catalogues
in prototype form. It will support data sorting and the production of graphs, mathematical or
statistical functions, and export to more specialized studies without requiring either new
training of operators or new programming.
  The resulting files, in most cases, will be small enough to be transferred via e-mail
attachments. They will fit on most electronic media and even on portable devices.

DIARY NOTE

Subject:  SA-5


1.  NASA provides bimonthly launch briefings to the Department of
State on all NASA launchings scheduled for the following two-month
period.

2.  The SA-5 launch was flagged at the briefing of October 23 because
of the large weight expected to be put in orbit and re-enter.  No
objection was registered by the Department of State.

3.  The following day, October 24, Mr. Frutkin called Dr. Golovin
to recommend that Dr. Weisner be briefed on the SA-5.  Golovin was to
arrange a meeting for this purpose.  A request for a briefing was
received from Dr. Steininger of Dr. Weisner's staff on December 9,
1963, and he was briefing that day by Capt. Holcomb (NASA).

4.  Prior to the initial briefing, NASA had taken two principal
precautions to reduce the total weight of fragments that might
return:  (1) 13,000 lbs. of sand were substituted for the ballast
originally programmed (lead and iron); (2) the Jupiter nose cone
was roughed up so that it would burn up during reentry.

5.  At Department of State request, a second briefing on SA-5 was
held on November 27.  No objections were registered to the launching
by Dr. Rollefson or his associates.

6.  The facts which were presented in the briefing for Dr. Rollefson
(subsequently revised as in Paragraph 7) are:

     (a) There is a 95% probability that 2,800 lbs. of material will
     return to earth, a 75% probability that 4,600 lbs. will return
     and a 50% chance that 10,200 lbs. will return.  The 2,800 lbs.
     would probably take the form of 30 to 39 fragments, consisting
     of six engines, three Titanium spheres and approximately 30
     electronics packages.  The difference between 2,800 lbs. figure
     and the 4,600 lbs. figure is in the Jupiter nose cone.

(b) It was stated that fragments would probably impact over an
area between 2,170 and 2,500 miles long by 100 miles wide.

(c) None of the aluminum skin material is expected to survive
reentry. Interior parts should therefore be exposed to heating
during reentry. (Most fragments collected to date have been
stainless steel pieces of Atlas skin).

(d) If 30 fragments reenter the atmosphere, the probability of
a casulty is estimated at .0000179. If 39 pieces reenter, the
probability is .0000232, or one casulty per 50,000 flights. A
fragment is considered capable of inflicting injury or death if
it hits with more than 58 foot pounds of kinetic energy.

(e) The nominal but uncertain lifetime projected for the satellite
is 148 days. The vehicle is to be launched on a heading of
105°, with a 345 nautical mile apogee, 141 nautical mile perigee,
31.60 inclination and a 93.9 minute period.

(f) NASA has investigated the possibility of destructing the
satellite in orbit. This does not appear feasible since any
destruct short of vaporization would simply create more fragments
of a lethal nature and increase the probabilities of a casualty.
In order to vaporize the satellite, a nuclear charge would be
required.

(g) At the current stage of engineering, it is not possible to
provide retro-rocket and orientation systems to deorbit the
satellite in open water. Some 18 months might be required for
this and the solution would not be applicable to future required
GEMINI missions.

(h) If the 13,000 lbs. of sand are subtracted, it is estimated
that the vehicle will be of the approximate weight and size of
Soviet vehicles which have already decayed. It is not known
whether the Soviets have taken any precautions regarding
fragments.

(i) A tracking beacon with a 45-day life has been placed on
board the satellite to assist in monitoring it as closely as
possible.

(j) It has been estimated that the reentry prospects here are
not greatly different from Atlas reentries in which about 2,000
lbs. per flight are believed to have returned to earth.

RESPONSE TO QUERY                                    April 8, 1964

RE:  Queries on Fragment Return from NASA Spacecraft or Space Vehicles


     A much abbreviated guideline for RTQ has been provided by Mr. Scheer
to various NASA officials who might be queried on this subject.  The
following more extensive responses are provided as background information
to be used by the Administrator, Deputy Administrator, or Associate
Administrator of NASA, in their judgment, in event of queries on the
return of space vehicle fragments to the earth.  It is suggested that
the minimum information be used to satisfy a given query.

(A)  FOR USE PRIOR TO AND AFTER A PARTICULAR LAUNCH BUT BEFORE ANY KNOWN
     IMPACT OF RETURNING FRAGMENTS:

     1.  Do fragments from (satellite X) pose a threat to life or
         property?

         The probability that fragments from (satellite X) may cause
         damage or injury is remote.  The probability of injury from
         natural meteorites is far greater.

     2.  a.  What is the probability of impact?

         There are many factors (e.g., time in orbit, atmospheric
         conditions, how the vehicle breaks up, dispersal pattern, etc.)
         involved and the calculations are extremely complex.  We have
         assured ourselves, however, that the hazard is far less than
         many hazards encountered in everyday living.

         b.  What is the numerical probability that NASA has placed on
             this?

         In the case of SA-5, it is one in 50,000 launches.
         In the case of GT-1, it is one in 27,500 launches.

     3.  Has NASA taken steps to lessen the fragment problem?

         Yes.  NASA is actively engaged in minimizing it.  For example,
         on the SA-5 satellite, NASA used 13,000 lbs. of harmless sand
         as ballast and roughed up the nosecone so that it would burn
         on reentry.  On the GT-1 spacecraft, NASA bored large holes in
         the heat shield to assist burning during reentry.  In addition
         to specific steps such as these, studies are underway to assist
         NASA in further coping with the overall reentry problem.

4.  How many fragments may be expected to survive

        From SA-5 - About 30
        From GT-1 - About 55

5.  If any fragments come down, where are they most likely to impact?

    The small number of fragments surviving from any satellite will
    be dispersed over an area of thousands of square miles, most
    of which are likely to be oceans, seas, or other water surface.

6.  Can the fragment problem be further decreased by exploding the
    orbiting element?

    Explosion or destruct of the orbiting element could produce
    more fragments and, hence, increase the possibility of fragment
    impact.

7.  If one were to be hit by a fragment, would it be lethal?

    In the remote possibility that one were to be struck by a
    fragment, it might, depending upon area of body struck, be
    lethal.  However, this is also true of being struck by a
    meteorite, and the possibility of being struck by a meteorite is
    greater than the possibility of being struck by a fragment from
    (satellite X).  In fact, based on data provided through the
    Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, the average number of
    meteorites over 2.2 lbs. which impact on the earth every year
    is estimated at 5628.  This is many, many times greater than
    the total number of fragments to be expected from (satellite
    X).  And, to date, there are no substantiated reports of injury
    from these meteorite impacts.

8.  Meteorites are natural phenomena.  Do you consider NASA
    justified in increasing the possibilities of a lethal impact,
    no matter how improbable?

    Many human activities carry with them a demonstrable probability
    of casualty--flying, automobile driving, golfing during an
    electrical storm.  But we do not stop driving, flying or golf-
    ing.

                              GUIDELINES
              FOR INTERAGENCY HANDLING OF SPACE VEHICLE FRAGMENTS


        1.  The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) is
designated as the agency responsible for receiving, [analyzing] and
identifying [any] fragments, or suspected fragments of space vehicles
of all types, including the contents thereof, which fall upon the territory
of the United States or which otherwise come into its possession, except
that the Department of Defense (DOD) is solely responsible for receiving
and identifying fragments from vehicles launched by the DOD.

        [2.  NASA will turn over to the Department of Defense (DOD) as
expeditiously as possible fragments which are readily identifiable as coming
from space vehicles launched by the DOD.]

        2.  In the event NASA should come into possession of space fragments
under the sole and exclusive responsibility of the DOD, NASA will deliver
such fragments as expeditiously as possible to the DOD.

        3.  To insure prompt analysis for intelligence purposes, NASA and other
U. S. Government agencies will [give] deliver to the DOD [and other
responsible agencies access] as expeditously as possible and on a priority
basis fragments (including whole vehicles) which are readily identifiable or
suspect as coming from [space] vehicles launched from foreign countries.
Such foreign fragments which come initially into possession of the DOD
will be retained by DOD for analysis.  Such analysis of foreign fragments
will be completed expeditiously, and thereafter such fragments will [remain]
be placed in the custody of NASA, pending final arrangements for their return
to the launching country or for other appropriate disposition.

        4.  All other fragments will be retained by NASA pending agreement as
to disposition.

        5.  NASA may continue to use the Smithsonian Institution for collection
and analysis of fragments by contractual arrangements, and may also make
appropriate arrangements for assistance with private agencies.

GUIDELINES FOR INTERAGENCY HANDLING
OF SPACE VEHICLE FRAGMENTS


1. The National Aeronautics and Space Administration
(NASA) is designated as the agency responsible for receiving and
identifying fragments, or suspected fragments of space vehicles of
all types, including the contents thereof, which fall upon the terri-
tory of the United States or which otherwise come into its possession,
except that the Department of Defense (DoD) is solely responsible for
receiving and identifying fragments from vehicles launched by the
DoD.

2. In the event NASA should come into possession of space
fragments under the sole and exclusive responsibility of the DoD,
NASA will deliver such fragments as expeditiously as possible to the
DoD.

3. To insure prompt analysis for intelligence purposes, NASA
and other U.S. Government agencies will deliver to the DoD as expe-
ditiously as possible and on a priority basis fragments (including whole
vehicles) which are readily identifiable or suspect as coming from
vehicles launched from foreign countries. Such foreign fragments
which come initially into possession of the DoD will be retained by DoD
for analysis. Such analysis of foreign fragments will be completed
expeditiously, and thereafter such fragments will be placed in the cus-
tody of NASA, pending final arrangements for their return to the launch-
ing country or for other appropriate disposition.

4. All other fragments will be retained by NASA pending agree-
ment as to disposition.

5. NASA may continue to use the Smithsonian Institution for
collection and analysis of fragments by contractual arrangements, and
may also make appropriate arrangements for assistance with private
agencies.

6. The DoD will notify NASA when deorbits are expected and
when collection teams have been alerted to obtain the deorbiting frag-
ments. Also, DoD will inform NASA of the results of such collection
efforts whether successful or not.

SUBJECT:  Guidelines for Interagency Handling of Space Vehicle
           Fragments


The President has approved the following procedures:

1.  The National Aeronautics and Space Administration is designated

as the agency responsible for receiving, analyzing, and identifying

any fragments, or suspected fragments of space vehicles of all types,

including the contents thereof, which fall upon the territory of the

United States or which otherwise come into its possession.

2.   NASA will turn over to the Department of Defense as expeditiously

as possible fragments which are readily identifiable as coming from

space vehicles launched by the Department of Defense.

3.   Fragments identified as coming from vehicles launched by foreign

countries will be retained by NASA pending final arrangements for

their return to the launching country, or other disposition.

4.   All other fragments will be retained by NASA pending agreement as

to disposition.

5.   The Department of Defense will notify NASA when deorbits are expected and when collection teams have been alerted to obtain the deorbiting fragments.  DOD will also inform NASA of the results of such collection efforts whether successful or not.  Any such objects obtained are to be returned initially to NASA.  Subsequent handling will be in accordance with existing intelligence collection procedures.

6.   In accordance with its statutory responsibility, the Atomic Energy Commission will participate in the analysis of fragments of space vehicles which have utilized or transported, or are suspected of having utilized or transported, radioactive materials, as well as taking res-ponsibility for the radioactive materials themselves.

7.   NASA may continue to use the Smithsonian Institution for collection and analysis of fragments by contractual arrangement, and may also make appropriate arrangements for assistance with private agencies.

8.   Upon completion of technical analysis, the State Department will provide policy guidance to NASA with respect to the return of vehicle fragments to the country where such fragments were recovered or to the country responsible for launching the original vehicle.

9.   NASA will serve as the focal point for the release of public information on such fragments.

MEMORANDUM FOR

          Honorable James E. Webb
          Administrator
          National Aeronautics and Space Administration

Subject: Responsibility and Procedure Re Space Vehicle Fragments.


It has been suggested that there is need for a decision as to what
government agencies should have what responsibilities in regard
to obtaining, analyzing, and identifying fragments or suspected
fragments from space vehicles which fall on U.S. territory or
which otherwise come into U.S. possession.

It has likewise been suggested that the National Aeronautics and
Space Council is the appropriate agency to work out a coordinated
position on this matter. There are legal as well as operational
problems involved, and hence it would be helpful if this combina-
tion of issues were kept in mind in identifying a person or persons
from your agency to participate in a meeting on this matter.

To the extent that agreements or recommendations have already
been made on this problem, information regarding them would
contribute to such deliberations.

I would appreciate your having my office (Code 113 - Extension 2203)
advised as to who would represent your agency. Such individual or
individuals will then be contacted for the purpose of determining an
appropriate time for a meeting.

            discernible.

            B-47, turned down and into the object.  The object proceeded to turn with
            the aircraft.  Pilot began to get suspicious of object when he was unable
            to close with it and it continued to turn with him on the turn.  The
            pilot knew there were no other fighters airborne at the time and other
            aircraft stationed in the vicinity could not turn outside the F-86D's
            turning radius.  The object passed between the interceptor and the city of
            Agana, Guam, and at this time no silhouette was seen.  The object proceeded
            south for approximately 10 miles at the pilot's altitude (20,000 MSL) then
            it climbed to about 30,000 MSL and came directly over interceptor.  Pilot
            turned aircraft to keep it in sight and it started circling him.  The
            interceptor was placed in afterburner and turned into the object trying to
            head it off.  It continued to turn around aircraft and he was unable to
            gain on it or close with it.  Then it proceeded west at aircraft altitude
            and returned over fighter at 10 to 15,000 feet high.  Pilot again turned
            to keep it in sight and it circled fighter again.  At this time pilot had to
            break off and return to Andersen Air Force Base due to low fuel remaining.

MEMORANDUM FOR DR. WELSH

Subject:    Conference with Frutkin -- Fragments

I saw Frutkin (and his assistant Marvin Robinson) for more than
an hour in his office on May 28.  It was necessary to review the
background and course of the meetings held last year because he
was away at the time and now is very negative on the project.

Frutkin seems to feel that:

     1.  No public announcement is now needed;

     2.  An Executive Order or statement from the White House
would scare people needlessly;

     3.  The problem is overseas and State would like to be able
to point to NASA as the U. S. responsible agency (without a scary
public announcement);

     4.  DOD and AF want to use NASA for a "cover" but have no
intention of letting NASA do anything but return some pieces;

     5.  CIA and NASA get along fine and can do so in the future
on this matter;

     6.  NASA should wait to see what the USIB settles on (and
would like to have us pass Frutkin's comments on the DOD
paper to AEC (at staff levels for information); and

     7.  Although NASA was drafting legislation, they (legal?)
would oppose sending anything up to Congress in the foreseeable
future because of the harmful debate it would touch off.


                         R. W. Hale

SUBJECT:  Retirement -- Colonel Howard M. McCoy, USOA, USAF

          1009th (IO) Special Investigations Group
          c/o Directorate of Special Investigations
          Headquarters USAF
          Washington 25, D. C.

     1.  Paragraph 25, Special Orders 167, Department of the Air Force dated 27 August 1954, extract copy inclosed, announces the retirement of Colonel Howard M. McCoy, effective 31 August 1954.

     2.  If retirement cannot be effected in accordance with these orders, a request for revocation of orders with specific reason will be forwarded by the most expeditious means to reach the Director of Military Personnel, Hq USAF, ATTN: Promotions and Separations Division, Washington 25, D. C., on or before the effective date of retirement. Orders may not be revoked if request is received subsequent to the effective date.

     3.  It is requested that you deliver the inclosures hereto to Colonel McCoy and advise him of the following:

          a.  His latest Report of Medical Examination has been reviewed in the Department and reveals no incapacitating defects warranting consideration for physical retirement.

          b.  Upon retirement, his final pay will reflect payment for all pay and allowances due him, including payment for unused accrued leave not to exceed sixty days.

          c.  He must furnish the Air Adjutant General, Hq USAF, Washington 25, D.C., ATTN: Personnel Records Service Division, by letter, his permanent address, name and address of nearest relative, and the name and address of person to be notified in case of emergency.

          d.  When change of address occurs, he must notify the Air Adjutant General at the earliest practicable date.

          e.  Certificate of Retirement, Report of Separation from the Armed Forces of the United States, and a new identification card will be prepared by the Air Adjutant General and forwarded to him in the near future.

MEMORANDUM FOR SECRETARY OF THE AIR FORCE PERSONNEL COUNCIL

SUBJECT - Colonel Howard M. McCoy, 550A, USAF

        1.  Attached is application for retirement submitted by Colonel
Howard M. McCoy for consideration and decision.

        2.  Colonel McCoy has completed more than 24 years active Federal
service and is eligible for consideration for retirement in accordance
with Section 5 of the Act of Congress approved 31 July 1935, as amended
(Paragraph 6a, AFR 36-50).

        3.  Colonel McCoy's request for retirement is based on the fact
that he has been assigned for the past few years in a specialized area
in the development of physical security and allied equipment and that
his military potential in any other field is limited.  He further states
that in view of the termination of this agency by the Defense Department
there is an even greater need for its continuation as a commercial
activity.

        4.  While he is recognized as a specialist in this former field
his overall military record indicates he possesses sufficient potential
to be of continued value to the Air Force.  Therefore, it is recommended
that his application for voluntary retirement be not favorably considered
at this time.

ATTACHMENT

SUMMARY:

     This attachment outlines the exceptional circumstances and factors
which dictate this officer's action in requesting voluntary retirement.1/
It reviews his specialized experience in the development of physical
security and allied equipment, which work has occupied most of his
time since 1946 and has made him the governmental authority in this
field.

     It further describes the results of an informal unofficial survey
he has just completed which accents the widely accepted need for im-
provement in our national industrial security program.  In view of
the recent abolishment of the Physical Security Equipment Agency of
which he was the Director, the most expedient way to fill the need
appears to be through the establishment of an independent civil organi-
zation working closely with the Office of Defense Mobilization and the
Department of Defense.  If this request is approved he intends to
devote all of his efforts thereafter to this important task.

BACKGROUND:

     The decision to take this voluntary retirement action was taken

only after the most thorough deliberation.  It has been the most im-

portant one made by him in his entire military career, and it is also

the most considered one, for he has been preoccupied with it ever

since 4 March 1954 when a Department of Defense Directive abolished

the Physical Security Equipment Agency (PSEA) of which he was the

Director.  He had been selected to head that Agency at its inception

and served for the three years of its existence.  During that time

the Agency became the recognized authority within the government in

the field of security equipment and it has an excellent record of un-

selfish service to the many agencies with which it was associated.

He had also been serving as Chairman of the Federal Committee on

Security Equipment since its organization in the fall of 1953.

     Since 1946 this officer has devoted practically all of his efforts

(about 20,000 hours) fighting Communism through technical means

by developing security and investigative equipment.  He consciously

selected this specialized field of work in lieu of a conventional career

in aeronautical Research and Development with full appreciation of

the lack of opportunity for advancement in the more specialized field.

He was firmly convinced that he could best serve the interests of

                              2
DOW-UAP-D180, Final Personnel Record for McCoy, Howard M., U.S. Air Force, 1954

national security by such action. He realized that: - Just as a nation's

organization for war depends on the technical weapons which are on hand -

so does a nation's facilities security program depend on the technical

security equipments which are available! It is estimated that less than

10% of the technical equipment considered necessary to implement a

realistic facilities security program has been developed to date. We are

in an advanced technological age yet our guard systems, both industrial

and military, have changed little since biblical days!

     As Deputy Commanding General (T-2 Intelligence), then Chief,

Intelligence Department, Headquarters, Air Materiel Command, for

the period December 1946 - August 1949, the undersigned managed a

specialized laboratory known as the Science Survey Office (SSO) which

developed certain classified types of security and investigative equip-

ment. That laboratory was abolished for unknown reasons shortly after

subject officer was transferred August 1949 to the Industrial College of

the Armed Forces. From there he was assigned to the Central Intelligence

Agency, leaving 1 March 1951 to become Director of the newly activated

Physical Security Equipment Agency. Copies of pertinent directives are

attached as Tabs A, B, and C. The need for such an activity as the

SSO had continued to exist after its close-out in 1949. The advent of the

Korean War so accentuated this need that the Management Committee,

Office of the Secretary of Defense, after detailed deliberations, established


                                    3
DOW-UAP-D180, Final Personnel Record for McCoy, Howard M., U.S. Air Force, 1954

PSEA to ensure extension of the work of the earlier laboratory (SSO).
PSEA was a joint project under the management control of the Depart-
ment of the Air Force with the responsibility for providing for the
development of physical security and related investigative equipment
as a common service for all agencies of the Department of Defense.

     It is estimated that PSEA had met only about 10% of its chartered
responsibilities during its existence.  There are several reasons for
this state of performance;  they include:

          a.  The initial small staff of 25 was never increased, as
     was planned, in proportion to the work-load that developed.

          b.  R&D funds for programmed activities were frozen as
     of March 1953 after less than two years of operation, the first
     funds not being made available until May 1951.

          c.  The Agency never operated under its revised Charter
     (Tab C) which would have insured full cooperation of the
     Military Services through the PSEA Policy Board.

     The Agency's efforts concerning security equipment were just
coming to fruition in the shape of a detailed R&D program, as the
result of almost three years of background research work, when its
untimely end came.  Government agencies other than the Department
of Defense which had come to depend almost solely on PSEA on
physical security matters dealing with improved equipment included
the GSA, State Department, AEC, NSA and CIA.

                              4
DOW-UAP-D180, Final Personnel Record for McCoy, Howard M., U.S. Air Force, 1954

The matter of the Agency's continued existence had been under con-
sideration by the Deputy Secretary of Defense since March 1953.  The
three Military Departments and the Office, Domestic Security Programs
of OSD, all represented on the PSEA Policy Board, are on record as
having supported the continuance of the Agency's activities, thus verifying
the need for its services particularly in the security equipment field
which constituted about 85% of its effort the last year of operations.

     The Agency and its functions were abolished 4 March 1954 per
Department of Defense Directive No. 5154.9 (Tab D).  Although there
was no stated reason, it is surmised that this action was intended in the
interests of economy for it is understood that some other activities were
stricken from the FY 1955 budget following the informal principle that
any R&D activity would be dropped that did not directly support a weapon
or weapons system already in or scheduled for production.  This con-
tradiction between the existing need for the Agency's services and the
act of abolishing the Agency and its functions, leads to the conclusion
that the Department of Defense does not consider the development of
security equipment to be its responsibility.  This apparently leaves the
matter up to industry.   This premise appears to be consistent with
administrative policy.

THE NEED:

     Assuming that the present policy of the Department of Defense in

                              5
DOW-UAP-D180, Final Personnel Record for McCoy, Howard M., U.S. Air Force, 1954

regards to its industrial security program is limited to the statement of

policies and principles, it is apparent that the most practical and sensible

way to fill the void between policy and an adequate working security

system in the defense industries is to follow the precedent of the Civil

Defense and disaster control organizations and have the Government en-

courage the formation of an independent civil project in accordance with

established principles of our competitive free-enterprise economy. Such

a project would eventually be a large one and should preferably be a non-

profit organization of the highest standards in the tradition of Air Force

Project RAND, the Battelle Memorial Institute and others.

     It is believed that the importance of protecting our defense industry

facilities (as well as our military installations) against sabotage does

not require documentation here as it has been a subject of comment by

the President of the United States, members of Congress, and other

Government officials for some time.  The Director of the Federal

Bureau of Investigation has stated to a Congressional Committee to the

effect that the technical problems of his agency have increased ten-fold

in the past one and one-half decades.  In connection with Mr. Hoover's

statement, there is substantial evidence that the USSR has spent an

estimated 50 times more effort in the past 20 years than has been ex-

pended in this country on equipment matters associated with those of

PSEA.  It is noted that existing burglary protection systems of the


                                   6
DOW-UAP-D180, Final Personnel Record for McCoy, Howard M., U.S. Air Force, 1954

central station type are less than fifty percent effective in preventing

penetration of the protected areas by unskilled burglars. On the other

hand, protection against thoroughly trained saboteurs must be near

perfect because the saboteur can be considered to have accomplished

his mission once the penetration has been effected.

     It is estimated that overall physical security in our key defense

industries can be improved in the order of four to five hundred per-

cent over a period of several years by the use of proper security

equipment and systems. The sums now being spent by the Depart-

ment of Defense for industrial and military security are described by

the Industrial Security Division (OSD) as "staggering" and are ex-

clusive of the security clearance program. The amount is classified

so it is not included here. A gain of several hundred percent in the

overall physical security of our Strategic Air Command bases should

be possible and would be of inestimable value. When it is considered

that it costs an average of $20,000.00 per year to man one guard post

in industry using civilian guards, and that military guards cost about

$40,000.00 per year per post, it appears possible to replace much of

this fallible human factor with advanced technological equipment with

a resulting gain in security, plus substantial savings in both money

and manpower.1/

THE REMEDY:

     During periods of leave since 4 March 1954, while acting unofficially

and solely as an individual, this officer has consulted informally with

representative industrialists and with casualty insurance and plant pro-

tection officials concerning industrial security problems and what an

individual such as himself might be able to accomplish were he retired

from active service.  He has also talked with pertinent personnel within

the Department of Defense and Government and from this research has

established that there is a nation-wide need within our Defense industries

for the formation of an Industrial Security Engineering Service (ISES),

or the like, to serve the same purpose regarding protection against

sabotage as the various commercial Fire Protection services accom-

plish in regard to protection against fire.  It has also been established

that no such service as an ISES now exists.  The reaction to his pro-

posed solution to the problem has been most encouraging and has been

accepted informally as being soundly conceived in principle, operationally

practicable and economically justifiable.  If properly implemented, it

has promise to fill a serious void in our industrial security program

which otherwise cannot be expected to be supplied for many years now

that the PSEA organization and functions have been abolished.

CHARTER

Physical Security Equipment Agency

     Pursuant to the authority vested in the Secretary of Defense by the
National Security Act of 1947, as amended, there is hereby established, as
a joint project under the management control of the Department of the Air
Force, a Physical Security Equipment Agency (hereinafter called the "Agency")
with the responsibility for providing for the development of physical
security and related investigative equipment as a common service for all
agencies of the Department of Defense.

I. DEFINITIONS

     1.  Physical security equipment is that used to provide warning of
and protection against covert and other clandestine activities involving:

          a.  Military installations and their sensitive areas.

          b.  Materiel.

          c.  Classified documents.

          d.  Personnel.

This definition is not intended to preclude the Agency calling to the
attention of elements of the Department of Defense applications of such
equipment to other than covert or clandestine uses or to deny the services
of the Agency to such elements in developing such equipment on request.

     2.  Investigative equipment is that required by the pertinent Depart-
ment of Defense agencies for:

          a.  Criminal and related type investigative activities.

          b.  Counter-intelligence and counter-sabotage activities.

          c.  Intelligence activities.

II. DUTIES

     Subject to the authority of the Secretary of Defense and in consonance
with the requirements of the various agencies of the Department of Defense,
the Agency shall perform the duties listed below:

     1.  For the solution of physical security and investigative problems,
review pertinent basic and applied research and development projects and
equipment, both domestic and foreign, and evaluate the feasibility of

modifying the equipment, or adapting the already demonstrated phenomena
and principles. (Note: Foreign information and equipment will be pro-
cured through established Intelligence channels.)

     2.  Experimentally produce prototype physical security equipment:

          a.  Based on requirements furnished to the Agency by the
              various agencies of the Department of Defense.

          b.  Based on needs anticipated by the Agency.

     3.  Experimentally produce prototype investigative equipment:

          a.  Based on requirements furnished to the Agency by the
              various agencies of the Department of Defense.

          b.  Based on needs anticipated by the Agency.

     4.  When required by the various agencies of the Department of
Defense, will with respect to specially developed equipment or supplies:

          a.  Procure service test quantities of prototype equipment
              and supplies.

          b.  Assist in the preparation of training and technical manuals.

          c.  Assist in training of personnel in the use of such equipment.

          d.  Assist in the maintenance of such equipment.

     5.  Furnish advice and assistance to other Government agencies on
the above matters as appropriate.

     6.  Furnish, when requested, advice, assistance and coordination on
matters concerning standardization, procurement, supply, operation and
maintenance of the above items which may be adopted by one or more of the
Services as items of standard issue.

     7.  Establish and maintain a working reference library pertinent to
the mission.

     8.  Prepare an annual report on its activities for the Secretary of
Defense and submit such interim program reports as may be advisable.

III. ADMINISTRATION

     1.  The Secretary of the Air Force, as Managing Agent for the Secre-
tary of Defense, shall be responsible for the operations of the Agency and
shall provide such personnel, facilities and other administrative services
as may be required to insure its efficient operation.

     2.   The Secretary of the Air Force, with the concurrence of the
other military secretaries and the approval of the Secretary of Defense,
shall appoint a Director of the Agency.  The Director of the Agency, if
a military officer, shall be appointed for a term of three years and shall
be eligible for one reappointment.

     3.   The Assistant Secretary of Defense (Comptroller) shall arrange
with the three military departments for the financing of the Agency.

     4.   In view of the high technical, security and urgency aspects of
this project, the Service managing the Agency shall provide all possible
freedom of action in the conduct of operations of the Agency.

     5.   Each Service may assign such personnel to the Agency on temporary
duty as may be required.

IV.  RELATIONSHIPS

     1.   The Agency shall coordinate its efforts with all agencies within
and outside the Department of Defense which have a mutual interest or
responsibility with respect to any of its programs.

     2.   The Director and the staff of the Agency are authorized and
expected to communicate directly and expeditiously with all agencies of
the Department of Defense and appropriate sub-divisions thereof, concern-
ing any matter within its jurisdiction and in which there exists a mutual
interest or responsibility.

     3.   Services of the Agency shall be available to all Department of
Defense agencies.

     4.   All agencies of the Department of Defense shall cooperate fully
in assisting the Agency in the performance of its missions.

     5.   Each Service shall designate properly qualified personnel at
appropriate echelons for liaison purposes.

General Joseph T. McNarney
Commanding General
Air Materiel Command
Wright-Patterson Air Force Base

Dear General McNarney:

          On 11 March 1949, the first class of the Training School of
the Office Special Investigations were graduated. During the
course, important assistance was rendered by Colonel H. M. McCoy
and Mr. Louis C. Gust of your headquarters. On 21 February 1949,
Mr. Guy S. Kidwell, 11 and Mr. Earl A. Underhill of the Scientific
Survey Office, Department of Intelligence, Headquarters Air Mater-
iel Command, lectured to the class on "Sound Equipment" and "In-
vestigative Photography."

          I should like to express my deep appreciation for the valu-
able aid and cooperation given by your command. The assistance
of the above-named personnel contributed materially to the OSI
Training Program.

                              Sincerely,



                         JOSEPH F. CARROLL

Subject:  Course of Instruction in Aeronautical Engineering at the
          California Institute of Technoligy.

To:       The Adjutant General (Through Channels).


          1.  The undersigned desires to explain in detail the course
of instruction he is undertaking at the California Institute of Technology.
It is requested that this letter be attached to his personnel file.

          2.  According to the provisions of Par. 44, Special Orders
No. 131, W. D. Washington, 4 June, 1940, the undersigned started the
summer course in aeronautical engineering July 15, 1940.  He had previously
in 1935 received the Master of Science degree in Aeronautical Engineering
at this school.  Upon entrance this past July he applied for and was
admitted to Candidacy for Doctor of Philosophy Degree.  Because the
regular summer course was too limited for credits toward this latter
degree; additional credits to total sixty-five (65) were taken and received
for the summer term.

          Upon detail here from the Materiel Division, Wright Field, Ohio,
he had been directed by Bridadier General (Then Lieut. Col.) O. P. Echols to
further perfect his knowledge of aircraft propellers, on which subject
he has specialized the past six years.  As there is no regular course in
propellers, and as he has taken the majority of the aeronautical subjects
during the year 1934-35 in addition to those subjects studied at the Air
Corps Engineering School in 1935-36, it was decided with members of the
faculty that the following schedule of subjects be undertaken.  This
schedule meets the requirements for credits for Candidacy for Ph. Degree
and permit specialized study on propeller matters.  It is noted that
although admitted to Candidacy that requirements for Ph. Degree can only
partially be met this school year.  Hence no degree will be received.
The schedule follows:-

     1.  Aeronautical Engineering Seminar.  )
     2.       "            "        Research. ) (Scheduled course totaling
     3.  Aeronautical Mathematics Reading.  )    45 units.)
     4.  Technical German.    (Regular attendance at this class. It is
                               required that a test be passed for Ph. Degree
                               but no credits are allowed Graduate Students
                               for class attendance.)

The research problem item No. 2 is "The Control and Syn-
chronization of Aircraft Propellers".

        The Math Reading item No. 3 consists of regular attendance
at four classes, auditing each for whatever pertinent information
concerning propellers in particular and associated airplane problems
that they may contain.

                Advanced Problems in Airplane Design.
                Elasticity Applied to Aeronautics.
                Theoretical Aerodynamics.
                Engineering Mathematical Physics (Vibrations).

In addition there is assigned and selective reading on vibrations,
acoustics and advanced mathematics.

        The above course entails a minimum of sixty-five hours of
study weekly.  Forty-five units of credits, however, are all that appear
on the records forwarded to the Adjutant General.  It was the desire
to explain this that prompted this letter.

        3.  It is requested that if the above schedule, which was
undertaken this first of three school terms, does not meet the approval
of the office Chief of the Air Corps, or The Adjutant General, that the
undersigned be notified prior to January 6, 1941, to enable him to
undertake some different schedule during the last two terms.

FOR THE EXECUTION OF THE OATH OF OFFICE.

1. Whenever any person is elected or appointed to an office of honor or trust under the Government of the United States, he is required,
before entering upon the duties of his office, to take and subscribe the oath prescribed by section 1757, Revised Statutes.

2. Oaths of office of Army officers should be taken before some civil officer who is authorized by the laws of the United States or by the local
municipal law to administer oaths; or before a judge advocate or acting judge advocate, the president of a general or special court-martial,
a summary court-martial, the judge advocate or assistant judge advocate of a general or special court-martial, or the adjutant of a command.
Officers of the Army other than those specified are not authorized by law to administer such oaths.

3. Confirmation by the Senate does not of itself continue in force a recess appointment and commission. A new and distinct appoint-
ment after confirmation is necessary and a new oath of office must be executed for such appointment.

appointment, return to The Adjutant General of the Army the oath of office on this form properly filled in, subscribed, and attested. In case

       Camp Silver Creek,
       East Tawas,                    Michigan.


     1, I desire to make a special report on 2d Lieut.
H. M. McCoy, Air Corps, on duty with this Company since
July 17, 1933.

     2, a, It might be expected that this Officer would
voice some complaint at the difficulties of flying
presented by his present duties.  On the contrary he has
showed initiative and enthusiasm in adapting himself to his
new assignment and adjusting his duties so that he can
arrange to fly when it is possible.
     b, With mostly voluntary labor he has constructed
a very satisfactory emergency landing field.
     c, As Mess Officer and Assistant Athletic Officer
he has shown ability which I would rate as Excellent.
     d, His initiative in relieving his superiors of
work and his ability to plan and carry out new projects
is Superior.
